en: *The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Dharma*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
The Buddha said: "First, for what reason does one practice counting the breaths? It is because the breath is easy to employ and easy to know. By means of the world..."

People of the present age all crave the body; they are unable to relinquish the body to guard the mind. Furthermore, the matters within the body are difficult to discern, and because they do not believe that [the self] is fundamentally non-existent, their minds do not cease.
For what reason is the intention of emptiness taught by means of "existence"?
Because one perceives existence and non-existence through the cessation of inverted habits, "cessation" (ānāpāna) is taught first;
this gradually accords with people's understanding. Starting from counting, once one has attained practice, it constitutes the first dhyāna.
The Buddha said:
"One should practice three concentrations when sitting in meditation.
What are these three concentrations?"
First, concentration of body;
second, concentration of speech;
third, concentration of mind.

The cessation of painful sensations constitutes concentration of the body; the cessation of sounds constitutes concentration of speech; the cessation of mental intentions constitutes concentration of the mind.
As for the cessation of thoughts, it means receiving and practicing the constant mindfulness of the Way;
as for the cessation of sounds, it means severing the four evils.
When pain and itching cease, one does not fall into greed.

Once the mind is established in cessation, the body becomes concentrated, the speech becomes concentrated, and the mind becomes concentrated; one should then establish the aggregate of precepts and maintain it with mindfulness.
"Upholding" means being free from all transgressions; furthermore, upholding through body and mind is called "remedy.
"Remedy" refers to the mental upholding and mental practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*).
The Sūtra says:
"That which is not recognized and that which cannot be stilled constitutes non-recognition within cessation; when the mind departs, one is unable to stop its departure.

Thus, one should apply diligence, exerting effort and maintaining vigilance. Sit upright, join the palms, lower the head, and hold the mind, fixing it within the heart so that it falls into its own arising and ceasing."
When you recognize that the mind is departing, once recognized, you should be able to still it; thus, you will not fall into the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
The hindrances consist of playfulness, doubt, and listening through the six sense faculties; such things are improper.
The Buddha said:
"In the practice of counting the breaths, the mind now counts the breaths without intermingling; what mental application constitutes 'intermingled practice'?
The Buddha said:
"Having attained the three concentrations, one's precepts accord with the Vinaya; this is the Dharma for the Path, the practice of loving cultivation.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"One who craves the Dharma of the Path practices the Path; having sat down, one practices the Path."

During the first watch of the night and the last watch of the night, one guards one's food with an alert mind; from the time of the *yuzhong* (mid-morning) until sunset in the evening, these are called the "four guardings.
One should remain focused and undistracted; this is what is meant by diligent effort.
Midnight, sunrise, midday, and the hour of *bhūṣa*—these are called the four right times.
One should read the sūtras, practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), circumambulate the stūpa both inside and out;

and one should observe one’s own body, internally contemplating the five aggregates of cessation, and externally from head to foot and from foot to head, observing each part one by one: what things are there?
All shall become putrid and decayed, with every limb falling apart.
Originally there was nothing that came into being; likewise, upon departing, it is extinguished and returns to nothingness.
Though one reflects on this repeatedly and applies the mind through counting, the consciousness still does not attain liberation.

When seeing a dead person with one's eyes, one should contemplate them carefully from head to foot; whether sitting, standing, or eating, one should constantly keep this in mind, using it to strengthen the heart—this is called "counting and recollecting."
When the mindfulness of exhalation and inhalation ceases, one has already perceived that at the moment the breath is extinguished, there is nothing whatsoever;
through calculation and reflection, one knows that all persons and things must likewise eventually come to an end.
"When the application of mindfulness is stabilized, one then knows emptiness.
Thus the Sūtra says:
"The first is diligent effort;"
"Second, frequent recollection;
third, contemplation.
The Buddha said:
"One observes one's own body; at times, one should observe the bodies of others. Observing one's own body is for the sake of comparison.
Observing the bodies of others is for the sake of detaching the mind from attachment to one's own body, so that one may observe the death and decay of the bodies of others."
At times one may observe one's own body, and one may also observe the bodies of others.
Observing one's own body is for the purpose of observing that the mind does not become attached to it;
observing the bodies of others is likewise for the purpose of observing that the mind does not become attached to them.
At times, one should not contemplate one's own body, nor should one contemplate the bodies of others.
One should not contemplate one's own body because of seeing it as fat, white, and beautiful;
nor should one contemplate the bodies of others because of seeing them as fat, white, handsome, with glossy eyebrows and ruddy lips.

Seeing fatness, one should contemplate it as bloated; seeing whiteness, one should contemplate it as the bones of a dead person; seeing oily eyebrows, one should contemplate them as the color turning bluish-black at the time a dead person is about to decay; seeing red silk-like flesh, one should contemplate it as blood that must all eventually rot and perish—what is there to be craved?

"This mind observes for itself that the body consists of thirty-two substances: calculating the eleven things—hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, skin, flesh, and the five viscera—which belong to earth;
the seven things—tears, snot, saliva, pus, blood, fat, marrow, sweat, and urine—which belong to water;
and the two things—warmth and that which digests food—which belong to fire."
Wind has twelve aspects;
these thirty-two things all arise from earth, water, fire, and wind. What is earth?

Human life originates from the vital essence of grain; grain constitutes the earth, intention constitutes the seed, and the vital essence constitutes the rain. Thus, through their union, the body is produced.
To seek clothing and food is to nourish the vital energy and protect the master [of the body].
The human body is fundamentally non-existent; therefore, it is subject to extinction and impermanence. Upon attaining the Way, one realizes that the body is not the self.
Contemplate that the body will not endure long and must inevitably perish;
since the mind is the seed of humanity, one must guard the mind with single-minded focus.
The deluded person does not guard their mindfulness or protect their vital spirit (ātmabhāva), but merely nourishes the four limbs, deceived by the flavors of form.
They reckon the body to be the self, unaware that all evils arise from the body;
they greedily crave the flavors of food and thus fall into suffering.
Coming and going through the cycle of birth and death without liberation, one suddenly encounters adverse conditions; the soul departs into emptiness, heading toward the paths of good or evil;
when the body dies and falls to the ground, it wastes away and decays day and night.
Furthermore, these originally do not exist; they arise as bodies through the activity of the mind.
Upon death, all return to the earth, and all things are likewise; everything must pass away—this is impermanence.
"Man does not calculate for himself; he harbors myriad thoughts, none of which are unified. He regards this as suffering, yet when his body dies, it is discarded and forgotten;
all things are likewise so."
Cessation is followed by renewed birth, and birth is again suffering; thus one plants the seeds of good and evil deeds, unaware of where one will go—this is what is called "not-self.
A practitioner of the Path should practice for the sake of severing this.
If a person does not understand the four types of impermanence, they will ultimately fail to attain the Way.

By reflecting upon one's own body and observing the death and decay of all things, one comes to know that both persons and material objects are entirely devoid of inherent existence; when the mind thus becomes stilled and restrained, one attains joyful practice;
having attained such practice, the mind becomes tranquil.
"Not being separated from the five [aggregates], his single-mindedness is the Way.
The Buddha said:
"Contemplate the body; observe the hair of the head and the brain."
Contemplate that hair has fundamentally no inherent existence from its origin; though it is formed through transformation, it shall all eventually decay and fall away.
The brain is like congealed rice gruel; it shall all become putrid and rotten.
The eyes contain nothing but the fluid of the hollows; they are all but liquid flowing from empty pits.
The ears consist of nothing but flesh, with their impurities all leaking through;
from the nose and mouth, mucus and saliva flow out, discarded and decayed;
as for the tongue, throat, lungs, liver, and heart, there is only foul blood within the heart.
The liver, gallbladder, diaphragm, and spleen adhere to the stomach;
the kidneys adhere to the spine;
and there is undigested food remaining in the stomach.
The large intestine contains feces;
the small intestine, like a bladder, contains urine.

When life ceases and the breath is exhausted, the abdomen swells and undergoes decomposition; the intestines, stomach, feces, and urine all become drenched and splashed together, becoming a foul-smelling and loathsome place.
Below are the buttocks, the two calves, and the two feet; the flesh and muscles gradually waste away, the sinews and veins decay and fall apart, and the skeletal chain disintegrates joint by joint.
The shins are rigid and firm, and the white thigh bones are like the spokes of a wheel.

The coccyx is connected to the spine; the spine is connected to the ribs; the shoulder bones are connected to the elbows, forearms, and hands. As the skin and hide decay and rot, the joints fall apart one by one.
The cervical vertebrae are connected to the skull; flesh and blood have completely vanished, leaving only bones that rub against one another.

When the breath departs and does not return, one is a dead person. The body remains upright and straight, no longer moving. When the wind-element departs, the body becomes cold. When the fire-element departs, yellow fluid flows out from the nine orifices. When the water-element departs, death occurs and one no longer eats. After three or four days, the color turns a deep blue. Pus and blood emerge from the mouth, nose, ears, and eyes, becoming bright red. The muscles and flesh decay, and the bones turn stark white. After a long time, they turn black and become dust and ash.

Looking at the stench of a dead person outside the city walls, one sees that the bones of the dead are like this, and one's own body is likewise; all shall perish and be exhausted—this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When the exhaled breath ceases, one immediately knows emptiness; knowing emptiness, one knows the body is empty.
"Why is this? Because one knows that life is near, for it rests upon emptiness.
The Buddha said:
"One should first contemplate and reflect upon this mind; by extinguishing discursive thought and awaiting the natural state of one's own mind, one maintains the mind.
When the mind does not emerge from the body, one is a practitioner of the Way; when it waits for things outside, it becomes the myriad phenomena."

When mindfulness is internal, it becomes reflection; when consciousness desires to cease, one must wait with mindfulness, reflecting that all things are impermanent and subject to decay, none of which belong to me, nor am I the master of these things.
"At the time of death, what does one carry away?
One carries away what is wholesome, what is singular, and what is necessarily maintained through the sutras; for these bring about much merit and much joy.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Take these things that are yours; all else is not mine. You should keep this in mind:
whatever is joined by affection must inevitably be separated;

each decays and perishes of its own accord. To dwell upon such thoughts only disturbs the human mind and leads one into transgression. One must instead return to the body to maintain purity and proceed toward the path of Nirvana."
"The Buddha, from the first stage of mind up to the ninth path, contemplates that the four colors must all be extinguished.
This means that when a person has been dead for four or five days, they begin to smell of decay and their color turns a deep blue;
on the fifth or sixth day, pus and blood flow from the mouth, nose, ears, and eyes, appearing a deep red."

Afterwards, the muscles and flesh decay and rot; worms arise within the intestines and stomach and devour them from within; the skin and hide dissolve and腐 (corrupt); the bones become stark white, and after a long time, they turn black and become dust and ash.
The elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space are all not what I intend for my own sake.

Since countless ages past, you have also served as a wife or husband, a servant or slave; you have also been born as livestock—oxen, horses, insects, or elephants—enduring toil and heavy burdens, and being slaughtered, flayed, minced, or roasted by others.

Now, having become human again, one further acts as a wife, husband, or slave for others; likewise, one takes the lives of animals by slaughtering, flaying, mincing, piercing, or hacking them. When these actions end with the death of the body, one must inevitably undergo the consequences once more.
"O practitioner!
Have you ever seen a dead person?

Once the breath has ceased, there is no longer any consciousness; the body lies stiff and upright, soon becoming foul-smelling, decaying, and loathsome. When one contemplates this clearly, it inspires fear and one does not wish to see it."
For what reason does one not fear single-mindedness?
Single-mindedness causes a person to ascend to heaven and attain the path of Nirvana.
Because the Buddha knows that the nine paths are all empty and non-existent, he returns to single-mindedness.

The practitioner of the Way must urgently extinguish discursive thoughts and wait until there is nothing else to know; then one arrives at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. While traveling through Kauśāmbī, one dwells in its midst, yet because the mind does not apply itself, one does not see.
The Buddha said:

"One should contemplate that desire and craving are subject to impermanence and decay; one should contemplate the antidote to lust; one should contemplate equanimity toward anger; one should contemplate the root of delusion; all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, while the unconditioned is peace and security."
If people do not understand impermanence, they will never cease their greed, nor will they escape the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
All that exists in the world is like a dream; one may see fine food in a dream, but upon waking, it is no longer seen.
All that exists in this world is thus: what is born must die; what is formed must perish; all things ultimately return to emptiness. What, then, is there to crave?
It is the same for people’s wives, children, and property.

Why is this? When people engage in worldly affairs and obtain profit from their wealth, if their families gather together in joy and pleasure, it is like a flock of birds assembling; all such things are impermanent, and once they part, they are no longer seen.
Even if one encounters anxiety, fear, and myriad sufferings while dwelling within the cycle of birth and death, these serve only to accumulate sins day by day.

A wise person restrains themselves through fewness of desires, seeking only one robe and one meal; they follow the practice of meditative concentration, not seeking a fixed dwelling place, constantly returning to maintain purity of body, severing craving, and contemplating emptiness.
He asked: "From what does the root of practicing the Way and guarding the mind arise?
The Buddha said:

"After heaven and earth were formed, humans descended from the fifteenth heaven; their lifespans were free from premature death, yet birth and death within the five realms of existence arise from the six sense-decadences."
The mind-nature of human life is inherently good; it is devoid of craving, feeling, perception, volitional formations, and consciousness, yet it is deceived by the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth.

The eyes behold forms; the ears perceive sounds; the nose discerns fragrances; the mouth perceives flavors; the body perceives cold, warmth, roughness, and smoothness; and the mind performs ten functions, thereby forming the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
When the intellect (*manas*) unites with consciousness (*vijñāna*), they become the six bases of decay (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
By performing good and evil deeds as seeds and planting them, there subsequently arise old age, sickness, and death, and one is born into the five realms of existence.

Seeking the Way in order to sever birth and death, one maintains self-restraint over the mind: one stops the eyes from [grasping] forms, stops the ears from [grasping] sounds, stops the nose from [grasping] fragrances, stops the tongue from [grasping] flavors, and stops the body from [grasping] tangibles; thus cutting off the six decays (*ṣadāyatana*), one practices contemplation with a focused mind, sits in meditation, and extinguishes discursive consciousness.
For one who has attained the Way, the five aggregates are entirely extinguished;
knowing that they are fundamentally non-existent, one then contemplates emptiness and proceeds directly toward Nirvana via the path of emptiness.
If one asks why one maintains mindfulness of the mind: it is for this reason.
The mind is the master of consciousness; because it acts, it is evil. The six sense-fields (ṣaḍāyatana) are the source of calamity; they plant the roots of the five destinies (pañcagati).

The practitioner of the Way contemplates with refined thought and maintains the four mental abidings (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni), desiring to cease [the flow] so that there is no depravity, for mindfulness, consciousness, perception, and volition run wild.

How does a practitioner who wishes to extinguish mindfulness, consciousness, and discursive thought proceed? They should practice the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena and sever the ten matters pertaining to the body.
Regarding the three—body, speech, and mind—they should cease from the five aggregates and the six sense-bases.

"The three concentrations are: when the mouth has nothing to know, it is concentration of the mouth; when the body has nothing to know, it is concentration of the body; when the mind has nothing further to contemplate, it is concentration of the mind.
The Buddha said: "The Way has four essentials; one must open the seal of the realm-holding [concentration] before one can emerge."
What are the four?
First, to recognize suffering and no longer turn toward the myriad things; this is the opening for escaping the three evil realms.
Second, to know that the body is not the self, thereby destroying attachment to the body and no longer craving it; this is the opening for escaping from the human realm up to the sixth heaven.
Third, knowing the mind of impermanence and no longer turning toward it—this is called attaining the eighteen celestial revelations;
fourth, knowing emptiness and the cessation of emptiness—this is called attaining the twenty-eight celestial revelations.
"Because the cessation of emptiness constitutes falling away from the Path.
The Sūtra says:
"The one who practices the Path and awakens attains liberation; that is, awakening to suffering as empty, non-self, and impermanent."
"Attainment" refers to attaining the four essential elements and attaining the first dhyāna.
In the seven heavens above, there are no physical forms or shadows. Why is this?
"Because practicing the Way destroys the body," *Faguang jing* (Sūtra on the Contemplation of Dharmas).
